I picked one up at a yard sale cheap but never tried it out. They fold flat for storage and are basically a metal box with an adjustable rack. Curious how well it worked and if the door-mounted thermometer was even useful? Also picked up a cheap Coleman propane 2-burner stove years before which I use often and wondered how much gas would go if both burners running? Made a simple dinner last night with it (canned beans, kielbasa, & corn bread), here are my comments -

  • Set-up is quick and once together it is very stable and strong. It sat on the stove without issue and stayed put.

  • Door thermometer is slow but accurate. I checked temp with a digital thermometer and they seemed to affirm each other.

  • Once near desired temp (~400°) it was easy to regulate and keep there with minor adjustments to burner valve.

  • Rack easily supports a 9" cast-iron skillet and you could probably get a 10" inside as well as a typical dutch oven.

  • The regulator iced up after 20 minutes use but the output did not seem to change. If it did it didn't affect baking time.

  • Both burners were on ~30 minutes and it used ~60% of small disposable propane tank. (A guess, not weighed.)

  • For the amount of output from the burner under the oven I was actually surprised there was anything left in the tank.

Oven performance -

The cornbread came out great. I baked it in a 9" cast-iron skillet and it browned nicely and pulled away from the edges. I added ~2 minutes to the recipe bake time as the temp in the oven dropped for a few minutes after the skillet & batter were put in. While the oven was coming up to temp I ran the other burner to brown the kielbasa chunks before adding to the beans (2 jumbo cans) to a large saucepan. This set at simmer temp the entire time the oven was baking. For all intents the Coleman oven worked as well as a standard oven. This was a real surprise.

Does it make sense as a prep item? It certainly does for me. We had a blackout the night before and sometimes we've been without power for days. The ability to make hot meals with some variety is a big plus. I've also become a huge fan of propane camp stoves. You can use inside without issue and the temp is as easy to regulate as a home gas range. The only issue is cooking area size and how large the pans can be if you cannot drop the lid flat. If you can do that any size pan or skillet works with most.

A word of caution. Propane cylinders should have a bit of empty space at the top to allow for expansion (~20%). A normal refillable tank has an automatic shutoff built inside of it to prevent you from filling it up entirely. 1 points nonrefillable cylinders do not have any built on safety devices.

So those 20 pound propane cylinders actually have around 25 pounds of space available, but automatically shut off at 20 pounds, allowing a 20% safety margin.
